## Two packages, one method

[ConvolutionInterpolations.jl](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl) is
the reference implementation, in Julia: the convolution kernels were developed there, and it
has every capability on this site. [convinterp](https://github.com/NikoBiele/convinterp) is a
port to Python, with a Rust core and a NumPy interface, by the same author. The port implements
the same methods — the kernels, the polynomial boundary conditions, the analytic derivatives
and integrals — and its test suite compares it with the Julia package across kernels, boundary
conditions, derivative and integral orders and dimensions; the boundary coefficients of the two
packages agree bit for bit. The [feature matrix](features.qmd) says which capabilities have
been ported so far.

The theoretical foundation builds on R. G. Keys, "Cubic Convolution Interpolation for Digital
Image Processing" (*IEEE Trans. Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing* 29, 1981), and
E. H. W. Meijering, K. J. Zuiderveld and M. A. Viergever, "Image Reconstruction by Convolution
with Symmetrical Piecewise nth-Order Polynomial Kernels" (*IEEE Trans. Image Processing* 8,
1999); the [theory page](theory.qmd) derives the kernels. The Julia package's interface draws
on [Interpolations.jl](https://github.com/JuliaMath/Interpolations.jl), where it began as a
pull request before becoming a package of its own.

## The JuliaCon talk

The Julia package was presented at JuliaCon 2026. The recording is a short introduction to
the convolution kernels and what they give — interpolation, derivatives and integrals from one
object — before the benchmarks on this site existed:

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QN3gvmk-WsE >}}

## Citing

If you use either package in your work, please cite it. Each release of each package is
archived on Zenodo with its own DOI; the DOIs below always refer to the latest version, and the
Zenodo records list the DOIs of the individual versions. Both repositories also offer these
details under "Cite this repository" on GitHub.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

> Bielefeld, N. M. (2026). *ConvolutionInterpolations.jl: high-order convolution
> interpolation*. Zenodo. <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23354656>

```bibtex
@software{bielefeld_convolutioninterpolations,
  author    = {Bielefeld, Nikolaj Maack},
  title     = {ConvolutionInterpolations.jl: high-order convolution interpolation},
  year      = {2026},
  publisher = {Zenodo},
  doi       = {10.5281/zenodo.23354656},
  url       = {https://convinterp.org}
}
```

## Python

> Bielefeld, N. M. (2026). *convinterp: high-order convolution interpolation, derivatives and

@software{bielefeld_convinterp,

## Declaration of AI assistance

Parts of ConvolutionInterpolations.jl, of this site and of its documentation were developed
with assistance from Claude (Anthropic); all code, methods and scientific content have been
verified and validated by the author. The Rust core and much of the Python code of convinterp
were written with substantial assistance from Claude; the mathematical methods, the kernels and
the reference implementation come from the author's Julia package, against which the port is
validated as described above. The author has reviewed and is responsible for all code.
